name: Dembow chops
rationale: Short muted chops on the reggaeton dembow pulse, grouped 3+3+2 sixteenths. The quiet version only marks the off-beat answers of the dembow; the busy one adds the downbeats and a little upstroke pickup at the end of each bar. Bar 4 pushes a ringing chord on 3.5 into the next phrase (quiet) or adds a sixteenth chop run before it (busy).

name: Ringing tresillo
rationale: Three ringing chords per bar on the tresillo (beat 1, the and of 2, beat 4), the 3+3+2 figure under latin pop and romantic reggaeton. The busy version keeps the three long chords but fills the gaps with light upstrokes. Bar 4 breaks into a short strummed fill that lands on a long upstroke or chord ringing into the next phrase.

name: Cumbia off-beat scratch
rationale: Light upstroke scratches on every 'and', the classic cumbia guitar answer to the bass on the beat. The busy version adds a down chop on beats 1 and 3 and a doubled sixteenth upstroke after beats 2 and 4. Bar 4 stops the scratching halfway and lets a chord ring (quiet) or turns into a short chop run into a pushed ringing chord (busy).

name: Cumbia bass and chuck
rationale: A picked bass note on beats 1 and 3 answered by short down chucks on the off-beats, with a skip upstroke after beat 2. The busy version answers every chuck with a sixteenth upstroke for a rolling cumbia drive. Bar 4 ends on a ringing chord on beat 4 (quiet) or a pushed chord on 3.5 (busy).

name: Bossa comping over a picked bass
rationale: Bossa nova comping: the thumb picks the bass note on beats 1 and 3 while the fingers place soft syncopated chords that change position from bar to bar in a two-bar cycle. The quiet version uses three chords per bar; the busy one five, with more sixteenth anticipations. Bar 4 leaves a chord ringing to close the phrase.

name: Slow bossa ringing chords
rationale: A slow, open bossa ballad feel: one chord on beat 1 left to ring, another anticipating beat 3, with a few picked high notes answering in between. The busy version adds a chop after beat 2 and an upstroke before the bar line. Bar 4 holds one chord for the whole bar (quiet) or adds a small fill into a ringing chord (busy); the quiet version also drops an upstroke before the bar line in bar 2.

name: Partido alto samba
rationale: A samba groove built on the two-bar partido alto feel: syncopated chords on sixteenth off-beats that answer each other across the bar line. The quiet version only states the accents; the busy one strums through the sixteenths with light upstrokes around them. Bar 4 settles onto a ringing chord (quiet) or a pushed one on 3.5 (busy).

name: Samba sixteenth drive
rationale: Driving samba strumming, the hand moving in constant sixteenths. The quiet version strums on the beats and the last sixteenth before each beat, like a surdo pulse; the busy one fills almost all sixteenths, leaving gaps after beats 2 and 4 so it breathes. Bar 4 closes on a ringing chord on beat 4.

name: Son montuno anticipation
rationale: A son and salsa feel where the chord for each bar is struck early, on the and of 4, and left ringing over the bar line, so beat 1 stays silent. The quiet version plays off-beat chops on 2, the and of 2 and the and of 3; the busy one adds upstrokes and a chop on the and of 1. Bar 4 pulls the anticipation back to beat 4 so the next phrase starts clean.

name: Clave strum (3-2)
rationale: The strums trace the son clave over two bars: three hits in the first bar (beat 1, the and of 2, beat 4) and two in the second (beats 2 and 3). The busy version keeps the clave hits as downstrokes and fills the off-beats with light upstrokes. Bar 4 adds a pushed chord on 3.5 ringing into the next phrase.

name: Rumba flamenca accents
rationale: Rumba flamenca strumming with strong accented downstrokes on beats 2 and 4 and lighter upstrokes around them. The busy version adds doubled sixteenth upstrokes after each accent, giving the typical rolling rumba drive. Bar 4 breaks into a quick run of sixteenth downstrokes, like a rasgueado, onto a ringing chord.

name: Triplet rumba with rasgueado
rationale: A rumba strum in a triplet (shuffle) feel: downstrokes on the beats and an upstroke on the last triplet before beats 3 and 1. The busy version adds a fast triplet flick after beats 1 and 3. Bar 4 is a triplet rasgueado run on beats 1 and 2 landing on a ringing chord.

name: Bachata picked and strummed
rationale: A bachata guitar part that picks the chord in light sixteenths with the bass on beats 1 and 3, and strums the chord on beats 2 and 4, with a light upstroke after beat 4. The busy version strums more, with upstrokes around the backbeat chords. Bar 4 lets the beat-4 chord ring (quiet) or pushes a chord on 3.5 (busy).

name: Bachata sixteenth pulse
rationale: A strummed bachata pulse where upstrokes fall on the sixteenth after the and, giving a lilting skip. The busy version doubles every group into down-up-up figures. Bar 4 stops on a ringing chord on beat 3 (quiet) or pushes one on 3.5 (busy).

name: Latin pop syncopated ups
rationale: A latin pop strum: a ringing chord on beat 1, a chop on the and of 2, and upstrokes on the sixteenths in between, so the groove sways around the beat. The busy version adds a second chop on beat 3 and pairs of upstrokes. Bar 4 ends on a ringing upstroke (quiet) or a run of sixteenth chops (busy).

name: Latin ballad ringing arpeggio
rationale: A latin ballad part: one chord per bar left to ring, with picked strings climbing through it. The busy version strums two ringing chords per bar with an upstroke before each. Bar 4 adds an upstroke on the and of 4 that rings into the next phrase (quiet) or a small strummed fill onto a ringing upstroke (busy).

name: Bolero with triplet flicks
rationale: A bolero-style strum: chords on the beats with a triplet upstroke flick before beat 3, over a picked bass note on beat 1. The busy version adds triplet figures around every beat. Bar 4 stops on a ringing chord on beat 3 (quiet) or on beat 4 (busy).

name: Guajira hemiola
rationale: A guajira feel in triplets that alternates two pulses: the first half of each bar groups the triplets in threes (strums on beats 1 and 2), the second half in twos (three strums across beats 3 and 4), a cross-rhythm typical of Cuban country music. The busy version fills the off-triplets with upstrokes. Bar 4 stops on a ringing chord on beat 3 (quiet) or after the cross-rhythm (busy).

name: Merengue chop run
rationale: Merengue-style off-beat chops with a quick sixteenth run into beat 4, giving the dance its forward pull. The busy version answers every chop with an upstroke. Bar 4 turns the run into a ringing chord on beat 4 (quiet) or a run of four sixteenth chops onto it (busy).

name: Vallenato paseo
rationale: A paseo feel: a picked bass note on beats 1 and 3, a strummed chord on beats 2 and 4 with an upstroke on the following 'and'. The busy version adds upstrokes before the backbeats and after them. Bar 4 lets the last chord ring from beat 4.

name: Romantic reggaeton long chords
rationale: A slow, romantic reggaeton part: one long ringing chord for most of the bar, then a short chop and upstroke on beat 4. The busy version phrases the ringing chords on the 3+3+2 dembow grouping with chops between. Bar 4 splits into two half-bar ringing chords (quiet) or pushes a ringing chord on 3.5 (busy).

name: Habanera strum
rationale: The habanera figure (a long-short-long-long cell, dotted eighth, sixteenth and two eighths) strummed twice per bar. The quiet version drops the last eighth of each cell; the busy one plays the full cell. Bar 4 stops on a ringing chord on beat 3 (quiet) or pushes a ringing chord on 3.5 (busy).

name: Baiao ringing pushes
rationale: A Brazilian baiao cell: a short chord on the beat followed by a ringing chord on the next dotted-eighth, twice per bar. The busy version strums through with upstrokes between the cell hits. Bar 4 holds the last chord from beat 3 (quiet) or pushes a ringing chord on 3.5 (busy).

name: Mambo pushes
rationale: Mambo-style anticipations: the chord is struck on the and of 2 and the and of 4 and left ringing over the beat, so the guitar always lands just before the band. The busy version adds chops on the beats around the pushes. Bar 4 breaks into a short stop and pickup (quiet) or a straight run of eighth chops (busy) before the last push.

name: Cha-cha strum
rationale: The cha-cha-cha step in the guitar: chords on beat 1 and beat 3, then the 'cha-cha' on beat 4 and its 'and'. The busy version adds upstrokes on every other 'and'. Bar 4 lets the last 'cha' ring (quiet) or turns beat 4 into four quick downstrokes (busy).

name: Latin trap half-time
rationale: A sparse half-time latin trap part: a long chord on beat 1 and a single chop on beat 3 where the half-time snare falls, with a picked high note answering. The busy version adds a dembow-style chop after beat 1 and sixteenth chops around beat 3. Bar 4 is one held chord (quiet) or a sixteenth down-up roll (busy).

name: Afro-Cuban 6/8 bell strum
rationale: An Afro-Cuban 6/8 feel in triplets. The busy version strums the seven strokes of the bembe bell pattern; the quiet one keeps only four of its anchor points with a ringing chord on beat 1. Bar 4 holds a ringing chord on beat 3 (quiet) or runs triplet chops onto a ringing chord on beat 4 (busy).

name: Chacarera-style triplet push
rationale: An Andean and Argentine folk 6/8 feel in triplets that leans on the second triplet of the bar, pushing ahead of the beat. The busy version fills each beat with a down-up-down triplet figure. Bar 4 settles onto a ringing chord.

name: Salsa guajeo with stabs
rationale: A salsa guitar part that picks a short repeating melodic figure (a guajeo) on the upper strings, with chord stabs on the off-beats. The busy version strums more stabs and picks less. Bar 4 lets a chord ring from beat 4 (quiet) or from the and of 4 (busy).

name: Rumba catalana fan strum
rationale: A rumba catalana feel: chords on beats 1 and 2, a skip upstroke and a backbeat chord on beat 4. The busy version is the fast 'fan' strum of the style, alternating sixteenth downs and ups with accents on the beats. Bar 4 ends on a ringing chord on beat 3 (quiet) or beat 4 (busy).

name: Latin house ringing off-beats
rationale: For dance-floor latin pop and latin house: upstrokes on the off-beats left to ring, so the guitar answers a four-on-the-floor kick. The busy version adds a sixteenth upstroke pickup and short chops between. Bar 4 settles onto a ringing downstroke on beat 3 (quiet) or a chop run into a ringing upstroke (busy).

name: Son strums with picked answers
rationale: A son-style part where a ringing chord on beat 1 and a chop on the and of 3 leave room for short picked melodic answers on the upper strings, as a tres player would. The busy version strums a fuller syncopated figure and keeps one answer at the phrase end. Bar 4 carries the longest answer.

name: Gentle samba-cancao
rationale: A gentle, slower samba-cancao: the thumb picks the bass on beats 1 and 3 like a soft surdo, the fingers place syncopated chords on sixteenth off-beats. The busy version picks the chord on nearly every off-beat sixteenth. Bar 4 resolves onto a ringing chord on beat 3.

name: Flamenco tangos backbeat
rationale: A tangos-flamencos feel: beat 1 is left silent and the hand accents beats 2, 3 and 4, a typical flamenco 4/4 phrasing. The busy version adds sixteenth upstroke flicks after the accents. Bar 4 lets beat 4 ring (quiet) or starts with a quick run of downstrokes on beat 2 (busy).

name: Latin pop acoustic sixteenths
rationale: A bright acoustic latin pop strum with upstrokes on the second and fourth sixteenths, so the groove pushes ahead of beats 2 and 3. The busy version doubles the figure with a chop on every 'and'. Bar 4 lets a chord ring from beat 3 (quiet) or beat 4 (busy).

name: Two-bar tumbao stabs
rationale: Chord stabs following the salsa bass tumbao (the and of 2 and beat 4), in a two-bar call and answer. The busy version strums a syncopated figure with sixteenth upstrokes that changes in the second bar. Bar 4 pushes a ringing chord on 3.5 into the next phrase.

name: Latin ghosted sixteenths
rationale: A syncopated latin pop and urbano strum where the upstrokes land on the sixteenth just before or after the beat, like ghost notes. The quiet version plays five strokes per bar; the busy one keeps the hand moving through most sixteenths. Bar 4 settles onto a ringing chord on the and of 3 (quiet) or runs sixteenth downstrokes onto beat 4 (busy).

name: Bossa anticipated changes
rationale: A bossa nova comp where the chord for the next bar arrives early on the and of 4 and rings over, with the thumb picking bass on beats 1 and 3. The quiet version adds just two chords before it; the busy one plucks chords on most eighths and some sixteenths. Bar 4 resolves onto a chord ringing from beat 3, without the anticipation.

name: Guaracha scratch bursts
rationale: A fast, playful guaracha and cumbia-pop feel: short chop bursts of three sixteenths on beat 1 and beat 3 with chops between. The quiet version keeps one chop per eighth around the bursts; the busy one plays the full down-up-down bursts. Bar 4 lets a chord ring from beat 3 (quiet) or 4 (busy).

name: Latin ballad in 6/8
rationale: A slow latin ballad in a triplet (12/8) feel: two ringing chords per bar with picked strings rolling in triplets between them. The busy version strums the triplet feel with upstrokes on the last triplet of beats 1 and 3. Bar 4 holds one chord almost the whole bar and lifts into the next phrase with a ringing upstroke on the last triplet (quiet), or adds a triplet fill onto a ringing chord (busy).
